historical_claims.anchor: A bilayer can form, and a closed bilayer can enclose a volume.
The fluid mosaic model captures the lateral movement of many components
The membrane is not a wall that keeps everything out.
Water itself can move across membranes, but specialized aquaporin channels can greatly increase its rate.
The language of hypo-, iso-, and hypertonicity describes water-driven volume behavior relative to a particular cell.
A membrane may have more sodium outside but a more negative interior, creating two influences that both favor sodium entry.
The sodium-potassium pump in many animal cells typically moves three sodium ions outward and two potassium ions inward for each ATP hydrolyzed
This is secondary active transport: the transporter itself might not consume ATP directly, but it draws on a gradient that must be replenished by some energy-consuming process.
In mitochondria, an electron transport chain passes these electrons through a series of reactions that eventually reduce oxygen to water.
The proton gradient has stored a portion of the free energy released during electron transfer.
Peter Mitchell's chemiosmotic theory, advanced in the twentieth century, made proton gradients central to the explanation of ATP production.
In plants and many algae, photosynthetic electron transfer in thylakoid membranes uses absorbed light to establish a proton gradient that supports ATP synthesis.

description: Follows osmosis, transport and ion gradients through membrane physics to chemiosmosis, respiration and photosynthesis, asking how cells couple reactions to useful work.
